newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Japan trade minister lobbies WTO members by mail.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade minister lobbies WTO members by mail.

text.p: In a sign of Japan's low profile at the first World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministerial meeting here this week, Tokyo's trade chief has been reduced to lobbying his counterparts by mail.

A ministry official said Trade Minister Shinji Sato has sent letters to about 10 developing country members of the WTO seeking their support for an info-tech trade deal which both the United States and Japan would like to see wrapped up here.
"The ITA (Information Technology Agreement) is the main thing for the trade ministry," the official said.

Japan's aspirations to be a major player in the world trade body whose virtues it has long touted suffered a blow when Sato was forced to stay home because of a domestic scandal linking bureaucrats at his ministry to an oil dealer arrested for suspected tax evasion.

Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda will also be making only a brief appearance here due to parliamentary business, arriving late on Monday and leaving Tuesday evening after delivering a speech and holding some bilateral talks.

High on the list of issues on which Japan would like to see progress in Singapore is the ITA, a U.S.-led initiative to eliminate tariffs on information technology products. Washington hopes the agreement will be the crowning achievement of the five-day WTO meeting.

Japan has already eliminated tariffs on nearly all of the key info-tech products, and as a major exporter of such technology would be a big beneficiary of more open markets elsewhere -- although analysts said U.S. firms would gain most.
U.S. and European Union (EU) officials met on Sunday to try to thrash out remaining differences over the deal to remove tariffs in one of the world's fastest growing markets.
U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said on Sunday that "important progress" was being made toward a deal, but declined to say whether a final agreement was close at hand.

A Japanese official told reporters Sunday evening that working level discussions among the Big Four trade partners -- the United States, Japan, Canada and the EU -- were "in gear" but also said it might be tough to conclude a final deal.
Japan would also like to see the WTO expand its agenda to include investment and competition policy, but key developing countries oppose such discussions.

On the thorny issue of labour standards -- another U.S. proposal strongly opposed by many developing conntries -- Tokyo has declined to back Washington but appeared to hope some middle ground could be found.
